facts.claim: JAA: a jewellery valuation (valuation certificate) is a document giving a detailed description and a value judgement of an item, based on current market conditions; the market it is prepared for (retail replacement, deceased estate, auction reserve and others) can vary significantly. Most valuations are produced for insurance purposes. Recommends jewellery be valued approximately every 2 years. (Same source and wording as sister posts: engagement-ring-setting-for-active-lifestyle fact_43.)

JAA: for a new piece, a retailer's valuation certificate is acceptable if it has a full and detailed description and the valuation figure is the same as the price actually paid (exception: genuine clearance sales). For pre-owned jewellery JAA recommends a registered valuer or checking the valuer's qualifications. There is no legal obligation for a jeweller to give a valuation certificate, and some charge a fee.

JAA: in Australia a person does not have to belong to a professional body to provide jewellery valuations; JAA points consumers to its member directory and to the National Council of Jewellery Valuers (NCJV), whose registered valuers must undertake training and ongoing professional development in gemmology, diamond grading and valuing.

JAA: a diamond certificate (grading report) from a laboratory describes the stone (clarity, colour, cut, carat, fluorescence, polish, symmetry) but does not ascribe a value; it is for authentication, identification and/or education. A valuation is a different document that ascribes a value. A diamond can be laser inscribed to link it to its certificate.

Moneysmart (ASIC), page updated 2 October 2026: contents insurance covers household items and personal belongings, including jewellery, if damaged, lost or stolen. When checking a policy, look at what items are not covered and whether to add items, for example valuable items like jewellery.

Moneysmart: most contents policies have maximum amounts you can claim for certain items (cover limits), so you pay the difference above the limit. (Moneysmart's illustrative dollar example deliberately not recorded.)

Moneysmart: portable contents cover protects some belongings away from the house; there will usually be a per-item value cap, each insurer has its own list of included items, and portable cover may be an optional extra. Most contents insurance does not include accidental damage cover; it may be added.

Moneysmart: most contents insurance offers replacement value ('new for old'); some policies pay the value of the item at the time it is insured, which can depreciate. When you claim, insurers may repair or replace items or pay what it would cost to repair or replace them (cash settlement). Settlement options are one of the features to compare.

Moneysmart: an excess is the amount you pay to make a claim; a higher excess lowers the premium. Insurers must provide a Key Fact Sheet with a government-prescribed layout, and you can download the PDS to read the detail of what is covered.

Moneysmart: list belongings with replacement cost and details such as serial numbers, receipts, photos, condition and purchase date; a video of each room creates a visual record for a future claim and helps prove ownership. Review cover at renewal (unreviewed for 12 months or more risks underinsurance) and add cover for special items.

Moneysmart glossary: a Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) is a document financial service providers must give you when they recommend or offer a financial product; it includes key features, fees, benefits, risks and the complaints handling procedure.

Smartraveller, updated 18 August 2026: always read the PDS before buying travel insurance; it sets out inclusions, exclusions, definitions, the claims process and emergency support. Some policies are country-specific, others worldwide; choose cover for every country including stopovers.

Smartraveller: travel insurance can cover replacing baggage and valuables if lost, damaged or stolen. Policies vary on valuables and often limit each item's value; check individual item limits on baggage cover, you may need extra insurance for valuables, and check the excess. Comprehensive policies may offer optional extras or higher item limits for expensive items; credit card policies often have lower item limits. (Smartraveller's indicative cost range deliberately not recorded.)
Smartraveller: insurance will rarely cover theft of items left unattended. Declare everything upfront when buying a policy or you may void it.

Smartraveller theft page, updated 18 August 2026: standard travel policies typically don't cover loss of items left unattended, items not stored in a hotel safe when one was available, items left with someone met on the trip, losses without a police report, or items stolen from checked baggage on an airline, train or bus or from a locked car. Consider leaving valuables in the hotel safe.

Smartraveller: report a theft to local police (local emergency numbers are in each destination's travel advice); you can't claim on travel insurance without a police report, and your insurer may ask for a copy. The Australian Government cannot help with an insurance claim or replace items other than a passport.

AFCA: the Australian Financial Complaints Authority is a free, fair and independent service for consumers and small businesses with complaints about financial firms, including insurance. The first step is usually to raise the problem with the firm directly. AFCA may not help if a court has decided the matter, it is outside AFCA's rules or time limits, or the firm is not an AFCA member. Prepare by gathering supporting documents.
facts.conflicts: AFCA is an external dispute resolution body authorised by government, not a government department; source_type 'government' used as nearest schema value.

facts.claim: Insurance Council of Australia: agreed value is a fixed amount you and the insurer set when you take out or renew a policy; market value is assessed at claim time and can fall. The ICA notes valuation disputes are among the most common complaints to AFCA (said of car insurance), and sets out the path: raise it with the insurer with evidence such as an independent valuation, then the insurer's internal dispute resolution (described in the PDS), then AFCA.
facts.conflicts: ICA article is written about car insurance. Writer may use the general definitions of agreed vs market value but must not say jewellery policies work the same way; jewellery-specific settlement basis is 'check your policy'.

facts.claim: ICA: the General Insurance Code of Practice sets the standards general insurers must meet with customers. The current Code took effect July 2021, updated October 2021 and October 2023. On 22 October 2026 the ICA submitted a redrafted Code to ASIC. Alleged breaches can be reported to the Code Governance Committee (insurancecode.org.au).

ICA Code FAQ (listing excerpt): the Code is voluntary and sets standards such as being open, fair and honest, and sets out timeframes for insurers to respond to claims. Specific timeframes were not read.

ICA Code FAQ: duty of disclosure means that when you apply for, renew or extend a policy you must tell the insurer everything relevant, or reasonably expected to be relevant, to its decision to insure you.

Carried from sister pack (engagement-ring-setting-for-active-lifestyle fact_40; engagement-ring-styles fact_49): GIA advises packing jewellery in carry-on rather than checked luggage and telling your insurer your travel dates.
Carried from sister pack (engagement-ring-setting-for-active-lifestyle fact_42): GIA advises checking that a jewellery policy covers damage and loss as well as theft, and reading it carefully.

Carried from lab-grown-diamonds pack (fact_11, fact_13, fact_24): GIA's lab-grown report confirms an item is laboratory-grown and inscribes 'Laboratory-Grown' on the girdle; IGI lab-grown reports carry an 'LG' prefix inscribed on the girdle; reports can be checked online by report number (GIA Report Check).
facts.conflicts: IGI wording carried from a search summary in the lab-grown pack, not read in full; keep it generic.

insider_details.detail: Ask for the valuation at the counter, not later: JAA accepts a retailer's valuation for a new piece only if it describes the ring in full and matches the price paid, so the purchase day is the easiest moment to get the document an insurer will want.

The grading report and the valuation do different jobs: the report identifies the stone (and links to it by laser inscription) but carries no value, while the valuation carries the figure. Keep both, plus photos and receipt, in one folder you can reach from overseas.

Diary the revaluation for every second anniversary of the purchase (JAA's approximately two-year interval) and update the insured value at the next renewal; it lines up neatly with booking a pre-wedding setting check.

On the wedding trip, the ring lives on a hand, in the carry-on or in the room safe: Smartraveller lists unattended items, items not in an available hotel safe and checked baggage among typical exclusions, so beach clubs, pool loungers and boat days are where cover quietly lapses.
If the ring is stolen abroad, get the local police report before leaving that town; Smartraveller says you can't claim on travel insurance without one, and consular staff can't help with the claim.

If a claim is declined or the payout looks low, the order is insurer, then the insurer's internal complaints process (set out in the PDS), then AFCA, which is free; an independent valuation is the evidence the ICA itself suggests bringing.
